system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2192-06-11 17:33:00 to 2192-06-13 12:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, prior stents, diabetes, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for pleuritic chest pain lasting three days. The pain was positional and worse with inspiration, differing from prior myocardial infarctions. Initial evaluation showed normal troponins, no EKG evidence of acute ischemia, and a normal echocardiogram. A nuclear stress test was normal, and imaging ruled out pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection. The clinical picture was consistent with pericarditis. The patient responded well to acetaminophen and symptom management, with no complications. Chronic conditions including diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and heart failure were managed with continued medications. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions for pain control, weight monitoring, and cardiology follow-up.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Chest pain.

TECHNIQUE:  Supine AP view of the chest.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:

Heart size is normal.  Mediastinal and hilar contours are unchanged, with mild
calcification of the aortic knob is noted.  The lungs are clear and the
pulmonary vasculature is normal.  No focal consolidation, pleural effusion or
pneumothorax is visualized.  There are no acute osseous abnormalities.

IMPRESSION:

No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality.

INDICATION:  Chest pain, elevated D-dimer, evaluate for pulmonary embolism.

COMPARISON:  CTA chest from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Contiguous axial MDCT images were obtained through the chest
during and after the administration of 100 cc Omnipaque intravenous contrast. 
Axial images were reviewed in conjunction with coronal and sagittal reformats.

FINDINGS:

CTA CHEST:  Pulmonary arteries are well opacified to the subsegmental level. 
Nonocclusive thrombus is seen in the left upper and lower lobar, segmental and
subsegmental pulmonary artery branches.  There is also nonocclusive thrombus
seen in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery, extending into the segmental
level, and within several of the distal subsegmental branches. No evidence of
right heart strain is seen. Numerous coronary arterial stents are
demonstrated. Thoracic aorta is of normal caliber without evidence of aneurysm
or dissection.

CT CHEST:  Thyroid is homogeneous.  There is no mediastinal or hilar
lymphadenopathy by CT size criteria.  Trachea is midline and airways are
patent to the subsegmental level.  The inferior aspect of lung bases is not
completely imaged.  Mild bronchiectasis within the lung bases is again noted. 
There are no focal areas of consolidation.  There is no pleural effusion and
no pneumothorax.

Limited view of the upper abdomen is unremarkable.  Bones are intact without
suspicious lesions.

IMPRESSION:
Bilateral pulmonary emboli within the left upper and lower lobar, segmental
and subsegmental branches as well as the right lower lobar, segmental, and
subsegmental branches.  There is no evidence of right heart strain.

HISTORY:  ___ man with bilateral PEs, evaluate legs for DVT.

COMPARISON:  Bilateral leg ultrasound ___.

FINDINGS:

Grayscale, color and Doppler images were obtained of bilateral common femoral,
femoral, popliteal and tibial veins.

There is acute deep vein thrombosis seen within the left common femoral vein
extending into the proximal and mid portions of the left femoral vein.  A
small portion of the thrombus is also seen extending into the greater
saphenous vein, just at the sapheno femoral junction.  The greater saphenous
vein demonstrates normal compression in the mid thigh.

Normal compression, flow and augmentation is seen in the distal portion of the
left femoral vein and in the left popliteal and tibial veins.  The veins of
the right leg demonstrate normal flow, compression and augmentation.

IMPRESSION:

Acute deep vein thrombosis seen in the left common femoral and femoral veins
and also minimally extending into the left greater saphenous vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Smith. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I understand you've been having some shortness of breath and chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started a few days ago—getting winded just walking to the mailbox. And the chest pain comes and goes, sharp when I breathe deep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Was the pain relieved by nitroglycerin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I tried it twice and it didn’t help. That worried me—usually it works if it’s heart-related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. You also mentioned fatigue and decreased exercise tolerance. Any swelling in your legs or recent travel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No swelling, and I haven’t flown or been on long trips. But I did notice a dull ache in my left thigh the other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for mentioning that. Given your history of coronary disease and prior pulmonary embolism, we need to rule out another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another PE? I had one eight months ago after back surgery. But this time I’ve been moving around normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re concerned—it might be unprovoked. We’ve ordered a CT scan of your chest to check for pulmonary embolism.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back, and I have some news. You have blood clots in both lungs—bilateral pulmonary emboli.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no… both lungs? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but not life-threatening right now. You’re breathing well—your oxygen levels are normal on room air, and there’s no strain on your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. But why did this happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. Since you haven’t been immobile, we may need to check for a clotting disorder later. For now, we’re starting treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting a heparin drip to thin your blood immediately. Then we’ll transition to Coumadin, which you’ve taken before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was on it after my last PE. But I’ll need monitoring, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll check your INR daily. Once it’s stable, you can go home with Lovenox injections as a bridge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we’re doing an ultrasound on your legs because you mentioned thigh pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You think the clot might be in my leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Sometimes leg clots travel to the lungs. We want to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your leg ultrasound showed a clot in your left common femoral vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the leg clot caused the lung clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. The clot in your leg broke off and traveled to your lungs. That’s why we start anticoagulants quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. How long will I need to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d usually discharge today, but I understand you’re still short of breath with activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just walking to the bathroom tires me out. I’d feel better staying another night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reasonable. We’ll keep you one more night to monitor and make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs look good. Your troponin was negative—no heart damage. BNP was normal—so your heart failure isn’t flaring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My diabetes numbers okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was high this morning, but we adjusted your insulin. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now therapeutic at 2.4. That means the Coumadin is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll go home on Coumadin 5 mg daily and Lovenox injections twice a day for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember how to give the shots. But when do I check my INR again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your primary care doctor will check it in five days. Keep taking both meds until then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also need to investigate why this happened. Your doctor may order a hypercoagulability workup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like a blood test for clotting disorders?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Since this wasn’t provoked by surgery or immobility, we want to rule out underlying causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re stable and ready for discharge. How’s your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still a little tired, but not short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Continue your home medications, including insulin, heart meds, and thyroid pill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nitroglycerin if chest pain returns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but if you have new chest pain, especially with shortness of breath, go to the ER immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Follow up with my PCP for INR and the clotting tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and cardiology too. We’ll send all the records over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Any chest pain or leg swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, everything feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable—heart rate 47, blood pressure 132/75, oxygen 100% on room air. You’re good to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, follow up as planned, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, prior stents, diabetes, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for shortness of breath, fatigue, and pleuritic chest pain. Initial evaluation revealed an elevated D-dimer, and a CT pulmonary angiogram confirmed bilateral pulmonary emboli. A lower extremity ultrasound showed an acute deep vein thrombosis in the left common femoral vein. Troponins and BNP were normal, and EKG showed no acute changes. He was started on heparin and transitioned to warfarin with Lovenox bridging. The patient remained stable on room air, with persistent mild dyspnea on exertion leading to a two-night stay. He was discharged home on anticoagulation with instructions for INR monitoring and further evaluation for an unprovoked thrombotic event.
